title: EMOTIONALLY ENRICHED FEEDBACK VIA GENERATIVE AI
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether adding emotional and motivational elements to generative AI feedback improves students’ experiences and outcomes in higher education. The authors focus on a key challenge in digital learning environments: feedback can become transactional and emotionally flat, even though students’ emotional reactions to feedback are important for motivation, engagement, and learning. Grounded in Control-Value Theory of Achievement Emotions, the study asks whether emotionally enriched AI feedback changes students’ engagement with feedback, their perceptions of its usefulness, their emotional responses, and the quality of their work.

The intervention was implemented in RiPPLE, an adaptive learnersourcing platform used in a first-year university web design course. Students were randomly assigned to receive either neutral AI feedback (control) or emotionally enriched AI feedback (experimental). The enriched feedback used praise, encouragement, supportive phrasing, and emojis while keeping the core constructive content similar. Large language models provided instant feedback on students’ authored learning resources and on peer feedback they wrote. The study combined platform log data, quality ratings of student-created resources, star ratings of feedback usefulness, a 41-item emotion survey, and qualitative comments analyzed thematically.

The population consisted of 425 students at the University of Queensland in Australia, with analysis using 381 consenting students’ platform data and 103 survey respondents. The sample included mostly undergraduates, plus a small number of graduate students, in an introductory higher education course where RiPPLE activities counted toward assessment. The intervention occurred over an initial four-week period for survey administration, within a course structure involving four rounds of resource creation, peer review, and drill-and-practice tasks.

The main findings were that emotionally enriched AI feedback was rated as more useful and was associated with lower negative emotion, especially anger, toward feedback. However, it did not improve overall engagement with feedback in a meaningful way and did not improve the quality of student work. Qualitative data suggested that many students found the feedback motivating and helpful, though some reported problems with length, redundancy, timing, and occasional inaccuracy. Overall, the paper concludes that emotionally enriched AI feedback can support student perceptions and emotional well-being without harming performance, but it does not by itself increase behavioral engagement or objective work quality.

identified_tools.name: RiPPLE
identified_tools.description: An adaptive educational system that uses learnersourcing, peer review, drill-and-practice, and integrated AI-generated feedback to support student learning activities.
identified_tools.use_case: RiPPLE delivered instant LLM-based feedback on students' authored resources and peer feedback in a first-year engineering/web design course. The experiment compared neutral AI feedback versus emotionally enriched AI feedback with praise, encouragement, and emojis.

findings.finding_summary: Emotionally enriched AI feedback did not improve engagement with feedback overall. In the creation task, the control group showed slightly longer median engagement time than the experimental group (76.545s vs. 70.6865s; p=0.026; |r|=0.059; N=707 vs. 696), while moderation-task engagement showed no difference (3.450s vs. 3.464s; p=0.920; |r|=0.00138; N=2709 vs. 2670). Survey-based engagement also showed no significant difference (Mdn=3.29 vs. 3.25; p=0.823; N=50 vs. 51).
findings.measure: Time spent engaging with AI feedback during creation/moderation tasks; survey engagement ratings

findings.finding_summary: Students rated emotionally enriched AI feedback as more useful than neutral AI feedback. For moderation tasks, ratings were higher in the experimental group (Mrank=190.74, N=103) than the control group (Mrank=139.79, N=91), p<0.001, r=0.289; for creation tasks, the experimental group also rated feedback higher (Mrank=54.43, N=42) than the control group (Mrank=43.89, N=54), p=0.040, r=0.206.
findings.measure: Student 1-5 star ratings of AI feedback usefulness/effectiveness
findings.sample_size: n=194 moderation ratings; n=96 creation ratings

findings.finding_summary: Emotionally enriched AI feedback significantly reduced anger toward receiving feedback. Median anger was lower in the experimental group than the control group (1.89 vs. 2.61; p=0.013; |r|=0.246), and the motivational anger item 'I get annoyed about having to address AI suggestions for improvements on my task' also favored the experimental condition (median 2.582 vs. 3.223; p=0.005; |r|=0.279).
findings.measure: Achievement emotions survey (anger overall and anger-motivation dimension)
findings.effect_size: |r|=0.246 overall anger; |r|=0.279 for motivational anger item

findings.finding_summary: Emotionally enriched AI feedback did not significantly affect enjoyment, hope, pride, anxiety, shame, hopelessness, or boredom. Reported medians were: enjoyment 3.31 vs. 3.12 (p=0.984), hope 3.38 vs. 3.29 (p=0.773), pride 3.42 vs. 3.31 (p=0.854), anxiety 1.82 vs. 1.62 (p=0.235), shame 1.71 vs. 1.46 (p=0.179), hopelessness 1.73 vs. 1.51 (p=0.452), and boredom 2.81 vs. 2.47 (p=0.212).
findings.measure: Achievement emotions survey across seven non-anger emotion constructs

findings.finding_summary: Emotionally enriched AI feedback did not improve the quality of student work. Resource quality scores were equivalent across groups, with both groups showing a median of 4.10; means were 4.107 (control, N=744) and 4.076 (experimental, N=751), with no statistically significant difference (p=0.470).
findings.measure: RiPPLE resource quality score (0-5) for created learning resources

quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled field experiment with a sizable sample (425 initially; 381 consenting for platform data), but it is a preprint and several outcomes rely on nonparametric comparisons and mixed measures with some attrition, so there are some credibility concerns short of blue tier.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention showed modest positive effects on perceived usefulness (r=0.206 to 0.289) and anger reduction (r=0.246 to 0.279), but no effect on work quality and mostly null effects on engagement and other emotions.
